note.text: The Caro-Kann. 1...c6 prepares ...d5 to challenge White's centre. The light-squared bishop comes out to f5 or g4 before ...e6, so it never gets shut in. Black aims for a solid position, not a quick fight.
2.Bc4 runs into ...d5, which hits the bishop and the e4 pawn at once. White has nothing better than taking on d5.
Now the e4 pawn is attacked. White must choose: push it to e5, exchange on d5, or defend it with Nc3.
Against 2.Nc3 the plan is the same: ...d5 attacks e4. After 3.d4 dxe4 it is the Classical again.
Against 2.Nf3, play ...d5 anyway: e4 is attacked and White must decide what to do with it.
Against 2.f4 the answer is the same ...d5. The pawn on f4 does not defend e4, and it loosens White's king.
With the knight on f3, ...Bg4 pins it and gets the bishop out before ...e6. Then ...e6, ...c5 and ...Nc6.
The Advance Variation. Get the bishop out before ...e6 closes its diagonal. Then ...e6, ...c5 and ...Nc6 attack White's pawn chain from the front.
Take on e4. White's knight recaptures, and Black gains time by attacking it. This is the Classical Caro-Kann.
Take on e4. The knight recaptures, and Black develops with ...Nf6, hitting it.
Recapture, and the bishop on c4 is attacked again. Black has the centre and an easy game.
The Exchange Variation. Taking with the c-pawn keeps a pawn in the centre and opens the c-file for Black's rook. The position is calm and equal.
Keep a pawn in the centre. ...Nf6 and ...Nc6 follow.
Recapture with the c-pawn and keep a pawn in the centre. After d4, develop with ...Nf6 and ...Nc6, as in the Exchange Variation.

note.text: Against Bd3, develop and hit d4. ...Nf6 and ...Bg4 come next.
Develop and put pressure on d4. Next ...Bg4 pins the knight that defends it.
Trade the bishops. White offers the trade, and without its light-squared bishop White has one attacker less.
Develop with a threat: the bishop attacks the knight on e4. Black follows with ...e6, ...Nd7 and ...Ngf6.
Now ...e6 is safe, because the bishop is already outside the chain. Next is ...c5 to attack d4.
Solid: ...e6 supports d5 and frees the dark-squared bishop. Next come ...c5 to hit d4, and the knights to d7 and e7.
Challenge the knight on e4. If White trades, Black's pieces come out easily.
Develop and guard d5. ...Bg4 or ...Nc6 follow.
Develop. White's bishop on b3 only hits the solid pawn on d5. ...Nc6 and ...e6 or ...Bf5 follow.

note.text: Pin the knight on f3, so d4 has one defender less. Black develops easily and stands well.
The same idea: ...Bg4 pins the knight and adds pressure on d4.
Pin the knight and keep an eye on d4. The bishop is outside the pawn chain, where it belongs in the Caro-Kann.
Keep the bishop: it drops back to g6 and still watches the long diagonal. If White plays h4 to chase it, ...h6 gives it room.
Now ...e6 costs nothing, since the bishop is already out and traded. Black plays ...c5 and ...Nc6 against d4.

note.text: 6...Nd7 stops Ne5, which would hit the bishop on g6. Then ...Ngf6 and ...e6 finish development.
6...c5 hits d4, the base of White's pawn chain. The queen and knights will add pressure on d4.
